Let [MATH: T] be the number of hours it takes bus [MATH: B] to catch up with bus [MATH: A.] Then bus [MATH: A] will have been traveling for [MATH: T+\dfrac{1}{2}] hours because bus [MATH: A] leaves the station [MATH: 30] minutes (or [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}] an hour) earlier than bus [MATH: B .]

We start by filling in a speed-time-distance table:

| Bus | Speed (mi/h) | Time (h) | Distance (mi) |
| A | [MATH: 40] | [MATH: T+\dfrac{1}{2}] | [MATH: 40\left(T+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)] |
| B | [MATH: 70] | [MATH: T] | [MATH: 70T] |

Both will have traveled the same distance from the station when they meet. Therefore, we can set the distances equal and solve for time:

[MATH: 40(T + (1)/(2))|= 70T; 40T + 20|= 70T; 20|= 30T; T|= (2)/(3)]

So, bus [MATH: B] reaches bus [MATH: A] in [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3}] hours. If we convert this time to minutes, we get
[MATH: (2)/(3)h|= (2)/(3)h × (60min)/(h); = (2)/(3)h × (60min)/(h); = (2)/(3) × 60min; = 40min.]

So, bus [MATH: B] reaches bus [MATH: A] in [MATH: 40] minutes after leaving the station. Since bus [MATH: B] leaves the station at [MATH: 9{:}30] am ([MATH: 30] minutes after [MATH: A]), it catches up with bus [MATH: A] at [MATH: 10{:}10] am.
